title: Too many open files error using temp directory on large CSV
body:
### What happens?

I have a Mac M1 Max with 32 GB of RAM.  
I wrote the following code that tries to do the following for each of 93 CSV files:

1. create a temp table with the correct column names and types;
2. copy a single CSV into that temp table, using the correct options; and
3. copy the loaded table back out to a corresponding Parquet file.

The CSV files have the following characteristics:

- 93 files totalling 750 GB uncompressed;
- the smallest file is 125 MB; the largest file is 40 GB; and
- about 20 files are larger than 10 GB.

For each CSV file, I run the following SQL code using the DuckDB CLI.

```sql
PRAGMA memory_limit = '24GB';
PRAGMA temp_directory = 'data/temp/';
  
CREATE TEMP TABLE t1 (reference_pool_id VARCHAR, loan_identifier VARCHAR, monthly_reporting_period DATE, <more columns>);
COPY t1 FROM 'data/stage/2000Q1.csv' (
  HEADER FALSE, DATEFORMAT '%m%Y', DELIM '|', SAMPLE_SIZE 500000);
COPY t1 TO 'data/parquet/2000Q1.parquet' (FORMAT PARQUET);
DROP table t1;
```

I’m able to run this code successfully for 91 of the 93 CSV files.
However, the two largest files - 33 GB and 39 GB - I get the following type of error:

> Error: near line 83: IO Error: Cannot open file "data/temp//duckdb_temp_storage-252.tmp": Too many open files

So, it appears that loading the largest CSVs via the COPY statement opens up too many temp files.

I also noticed some other interesting behavior with the temp files.
During the run, the temp directory grows to about 300 GB and 252 files, then duckdb crashes.
I don’t have any idea why a 30GB CSV file generates over 300GB of temp files and a crash.



### To Reproduce

Unfortunately, the data is proprietary.  I don't have time to figure out how to simulate a similar sized CSV using faker or the like; my apologies.  I just thought that I should report the "too many temp files" error, since most current use cases may not use such large files.  Thanks for all the hard work on DuckDB!

### OS:

macOS Ventura 13.4.1

### DuckDB Version:

0.8.1

### DuckDB Client:

DuckDB CLI

### Full Name:

Kyle Lundstedt

### Affiliation:

IndustryVault

### Have you tried this on the latest `main` branch?

I have tested with a main build

### Have you tried the steps to reproduce? Do they include all relevant data and configuration? Does the issue you report still appear there?

- [X] Yes, I have

There's a new (thoroughly) reworked CSV reader coming in a few weeks (as part of 0.9.0), so you may want to also try that once it comes out.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Thanks for the quick replies @participant1 and @participant2!

Here's what I've found.

Setting `parallel = false` in the `read_csv_auto` function does allow me to load the two largest CSVs via the COPY statement.  However, if I try to expand the copy statement to multiple files (e.g., `COPY t1 FROM 'data/stage/2*.csv'`, then I still get the "too many temp files" error.

If I add `set threads = 1;`, then my code works for the largest CSVs as well.  However, when expanding it to multiple files, the DuckDB CLI just crashes.  Adding `parallel = false` does not seem to make a difference here.

With threads still = 1, if I go straight from CSV to parquet (e.g., `copy (select column from 'a.csv') to 'a.parquet'`), I'm able to copy ALL the CSVs into a single parquet table.  Nice!

However, it does take about 4 hours on my M1 Max laptop due to single threading.  Also, I could not get the COLUMNS struct that I tried to add (e.g., COLUMNS = {'reference_pool_id': 'VARCHAR', 'loan_identifier': 'VARCHAR', ...}`) to work for the CSV reader.  Thus my big parquet table didn't have the desired column names and types.

I appreciate the help from both of you, and think that I can muddy along with `set threads = 1` for now.  I'm looking forward to DuckDB 0.9 and the reworked CSV reader.

So appreciative of this great piece of software!

Good news and bad news.

I downloaded v0.9.0, hot off the presses, and tried re-running the query that worked in v0.8.1 on the smaller data set with THREADS = 1.

The good news is that, using 0.9.0, this query still works when run on four files and DOES NOT need THREADS = 1.  Hooray!

```sql

PRAGMA temp_directory = 'data/temp/';
COPY (
  SELECT column000::VARCHAR reference_pool_id, column001::VARCHAR loan_identifier, column002::DATE monthly_reporting_period, ... column093::VARCHAR "index", ...

	  HEADER = FALSE, DATEFORMAT = '%m%Y', DELIM = '|', SAMPLE_SIZE = 500000)
) TO 'data/public/performance.parquet' (FORMAT PARQUET);  
```

The bad news is that, using 0.9.0, this query does not run when expanding the glob from four files (2000*.csv) to forty files (200*.csv).  I get this error:

```
Error: Out of Memory Error: failed to allocate data of size 36.6MB (27.4GB/27.4GB used)
```

Given the "out of memory" problem, it's not clear whether 0.9.0 fixes the "Conversion error" reported above.

No temp files get generated, and I can't figure out why I'd run out of memory.  Is duckdb trying to load all forty files into memory somehow?

Just in case, I tried running the same SQL from within a duckdb database (e.g., running `duckdb performance.db` at the CLI, and executing the SQL therein).  I get the same Out of Memory error.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
I want to separate out the "out of memory" (o.o.m.) issues from the "Conversion error" issues.  So, I went back to the simplest form of the code that uses ALL_VARCHAR = 1 to eliminate potential Conversion error issues.  

I also went back to the shortest version of the code, which tries to read all 93 files (750 GB total) using `read_csv_auto` and simultaneously output them in a single step to Parquet.  Based on the Parquet tips in the docs, I also added PER_THREAD_OUTPUT TRUE.

The code looks like the following:
```
SET THREADS = 1;
PRAGMA MEMORY_LIMIT = '4GB';
COPY (
  SELECT * FROM read_csv_auto('data/stage/*.csv',
	  HEADER = FALSE, DATEFORMAT = '%m%Y', DELIM = '|', ALL_VARCHAR = 1)
) TO 'data/public/performance' (
    FORMAT PARQUET, PER_THREAD_OUTPUT TRUE); 
```

I ran several combinations of THREADS and MEMORY_LIMIT to see what happens.  I got the following results:

```
-- THREADS = 1, MEMORY_LIMIT = '4GB': 170 min
-- THREADS = 2, MEMORY_LIMIT = '4GB': 90 min
-- THREADS = 4, MEMORY_LIMIT = '4GB': 48 min
-- THREADS = 4, MEMORY_LIMIT = '6GB': 48 min
-- THREADS = 6, MEMORY_LIMIT = '4GB': o.o.m.
-- THREADS = 6, MEMORY_LIMIT = '6GB': o.o.m.
-- THREADS = 8, MEMORY_LIMIT = '2GB': o.o.m.
-- THREADS = 8, MEMORY_LIMIT = '4GB': o.o.m.
```

So, it's nice to see that several combinations actually work using ALL_VARCHAR = 1 and PER_THREAD_OUTPUT = TRUE!

However, it seems like I can't run more than 4 threads without running out of memory, even though my Mac could run up to 10 threads.

Also, increasing the MEMORY_LIMIT from 4GB to 6GB had no impact on the runtime, holding THREADS constant at 4.

So, I can solve the o.o.m. error by using only 4 threads, but I really would appreciate it if anyone could educate me as to why that is the limit in this case.

I'll do some experiments on the "Conversion Error" tomorrow.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Good news; **v0.9.1 solves the remaining out-of-memory issues**.  (I'm still using `ALL_VARCHAR = 1` to avoid the "Conversion error" issue.)

```
COPY (
  SELECT *
  FROM read_csv_auto('data/stage/*.csv',
  	 HEADER = FALSE, DATEFORMAT = '%m%Y', DELIM = '|', ALL_VARCHAR = 1)
) TO 'data/public/performance' (
    FORMAT PARQUET, PER_THREAD_OUTPUT TRUE);
```

With 0.9.1, there's no need to set either THREADS or MEMORY_LIMIT.  Based on some testing, it looks like the "no THREADS or MEMORY_LIMIT" option is  equivalent to running with `THREADS = 8, MEMORY_LIMIT = '4GB'`.  Both version runs in 26 minutes, use about 18GB RAM at peak, and do not use any temp files.  

Increasing the MEMORY_LIMIT has no impact.  

The `PER_THREAD_OUTPUT TRUE` is **critical**.  Not using that option causes the out-of-memory issue to return.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Given the out-of-memory issue is solved by 0.9.1, I also want to see if the "Conversion error" issue is solved too.

To establish a benchmark using 0.9.1, I went back to the "three step" process of first creating a table in a permanent database with the correct columns and types, then copying all the CSV files into the table, then copying the table into a Parquet file.

```
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE t1 (reference_pool_id VARCHAR, loan_identifier VARCHAR, monthly_reporting_period DATE, <more columns>);
COPY t1 FROM 'data/stage/*.csv' (
  HEADER FALSE, DATEFORMAT '%m%Y', DELIM '|', SAMPLE_SIZE 500000);
COPY t1 TO 'data/public/t1.parquet' (FORMAT PARQUET, PER_THREAD_OUTPUT TRUE);
```

Using 0.9.1, this "three step" code executes perfectly with no "Conversion error" issues; nice!  The overall permanent database file is around 105 GB, and the run produces a 43 GB Parquet file(s) in about 2 hours.  In particular, the first COPY has no problems in loading all 93 CSV files into the pre-defined DuckDB table.

Now, I want to see if I can consolidate the "three step" process into the more efficient "one step" process.

```
COPY (
  SELECT column000::VARCHAR reference_pool_id, column001::VARCHAR loan_identifier, column002::DATE monthly_reporting_period, <more columns> column093::VARCHAR "index", , <more columns>
  FROM read_csv_auto('data/stage/*.csv',
	  HEADER = FALSE, DATEFORMAT = '%m%Y', DELIM = '|', SAMPLE_SIZE = 500000)
) TO 'data/public/t1.parquet' (FORMAT PARQUET, PER_THREAD_OUTPUT TRUE);  
```

Unfortunately, the "Conversion error" pops back up.

```
Error: near line 7: Conversion Error: date field value out of range: "062015", expected format is (YYYY-MM-DD)
```

I can't figure out why the "three step" code works fine, the "single step" code version using ALL_VARCHAR = 1 works fine, but the "single step" code version using column names and types in the SELECT clause does not work.

Wow!  I re-tried the "single step" code, changing the syntax per @participant2's suggestion.  Given I'm using the COLUMNS option, I changed the function from `read_csv_auto` to `read_csv`.  Here's the code:

```

  select * from read_csv('data/stage/*.csv',
    HEADER = FALSE, DATEFORMAT = '%m%Y', DELIM = '|',
    COLUMNS = {'reference_pool_id': 'VARCHAR', <more columns>} )

    FORMAT PARQUET, PER_THREAD_OUTPUT TRUE);
```

Summarizing the results:

- I'm using Mac M1 Max (10 cores) with 32 GB of RAM, running DuckDB 0.9.1.
- I'm converting 93 CSV files (750 GB uncompressed) to Parquet, writing an output file per thread.
- My code snippet runs in **22 minutes**, and produces a 43 GB Parquet folder (10 files, 1 per thread).

Many thanks to @participant2, @participant1, @participant3, and @participant4 for their help in sorting through the out-of-memory and conversion date issues here.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Whoops; spoke (closed) too soon!

The previous [code snippet](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/issues/8690#issuecomment-1767013277) works great when you use the PER_THREAD_OUTPUT option.  The Parquet output is split into 10 files, corresponding to the 10 threads I can run on my Mac.  However, I realized that randomly outputting records into those 10 Parquet files is not what I want.

I want to take advantage of DuckDB's filter pushdown when reading the Parquet files, so I need to do a partitioned write.  Unfortunately, I discovered that you can't use PER_THREAD_OUTPUT simultaneously with PARTITION_BY.

First, I naively tried to partition by 'monthly_reporting_period', replacing `PER_THREAD_OUTPUT` in the code with `PARTITION_BY (monthly_reporting_period)`.

```
copy (
  select * from read_csv('data/stage/*.csv',
    HEADER = FALSE, DATEFORMAT = '%m%Y', DELIM = '|',
    COLUMNS = {'reference_pool_id': 'VARCHAR', <more columns>} )
) to 'data/public/performance' (
    FORMAT PARQUET, PARTITION_BY (monthly_reporting_period));
```

Unfortunately, there are 279 distinct monthly reporting periods in the data.  So, when I run the modified code above, it eats up more than 1 TB of disk space (all I've got!) and the job dies.  If I run the same code for just four of the CSV files (about 7 GB uncompressed), the database .tmp file grows to over 58 GB!  So, the native partitioning strategy just isn't practical in this case.

Alternatively, I could partition annually, rather than monthly, which reduces the distinct files to 23.  However, when I try to modify the above code to `PARTITION_BY ( year(monthly_reporting_period) )`, I get a syntax error.

Is the explosion in the size of the database .tmp file something that is expected?  Is there a different syntax that's possible for use in the PARTITION_BY function?

In both cases, the permanent database file `file.db` creates a `file.db.tmp` folder when the code first runs. Then, the code gets about 15-20% completed, then the job runs out of hard disk space. Within the `file.db.tmp` folder, regardless of how I partition, the code generates a series of .tmp files where each .tmp file appears to be about twice as big as the last .tmp file. See below for an example: I'm no database expert, but I do find it strange that this process appears to require multiple TBs to complete; particularly, given the "non-partitioned" version uses only ~50 GB. If this behavior is expected, I'll just have to buy a bigger external hard drive. :). I appreciate any insight you can offer.
